title: The Tanya
hookLine: Shneur Zalman's book on the "in-between" person, neither saint nor sinner

cards: In the Talmud, a great sage named Rabbah says something about himself. The sages have just divided people into three kinds: the righteous, the wicked, and the ones in between.

And Rabbah says, people like me are the in-between ones. Abaye answers, half in protest: if you are only in between, master, you leave no room for anyone else to live. That short exchange became the seed of a book.
Rabbi Shneur Zalman, whose Chabad path we met yesterday, wrote it for ordinary people trying to serve God in a real life. It's known by its first word, and that word is today's.

teach.h: THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.
teach.b: Tanya. It's the opening word of the book, an Aramaic word that introduces a teaching of the sages. The book is also called Likkutei Amarim, collected sayings.
First, its promise. The title page leans on a verse from Deuteronomy: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Very near.
Not only for saints. The book sets out to show how. Second, the twist.
The in-between person, the beinoni, is not who you'd expect.
You might think it means someone who sins half the time and does good the other half. The Tanya says no. Its beinoni never actually does the wrong thing, in deed or word.

teach.h: THE PULL STAYS, AND IS NOT OBEYED.
teach.b: The pull is still there every day, the bad thought still rises, and every day it is not obeyed. Third, the comfort. If that inner pull never goes away, it doesn't mean you're failing.
That is simply what the in-between life feels like. And the Tanya presents this level as one within reach, not reserved for rare souls. Fourth, the week.
Look at this week's threads: clinging to God through a chore, joy that opens, a rebbe who guides, the body that serves, the self that steps aside, the mind that leads.
The Tanya ties threads like these into a plan for an ordinary day, for a person who is neither saint nor sinner, and still at work.

how: In Chabad communities the Tanya is studied daily in short portions, often alongside the weekly Torah reading, and its chapters on the in-between person are taught as a guide for ordinary religious life.

games.q: the sages divide people into righteous, wicked and in between. Rabbah, a great sage, says which he is. what does he say?
games.why: he says people like him are in between, and his colleague protests that this leaves no room for anyone else to live.

practice: Bring to mind one pull in you that hasn't gone away, a temper, a craving, a habit of the mind, and just see it, without scolding it or pretending it isn't there.

Then remember the times you didn't follow it, even once: the pull is real, and you are still the one choosing. If you pray, you can hold the verse: the word is very near, in your mouth and in your heart.
